figures.caption: Figure 5: IVOT versus IVMTE identified sets for the policy-relevant treatment effect PRTEα = E[Y qα − Y ]/α of a price subsidy of magnitude α on bed net usage, using data from Dupas [2014a]. IVMTE is reported for two u-spline sieves, degree 10 (orange) and degree 20 (red); the degree-20 bound is visibly wider, reflecting the more nonparametric MTR class. Shaded ribbons show 95% CIs: light orange for IVMTE (degree 20) and light blue for IVOT. IVOT substantially tightens the identified set and achieves near-point identification at several subsidy levels.

Figure 1: Bounds of the moment relaxation approach and the CCOT approach by different sample sizes. Each data point is an average of 20 runs. In the experiment M = 1, i.e., ymax = 1, ymin = −1.

Figure 3: Decomposition of the unit interval [0, 1] for the sharp lower bound in the continuous instrument setting (Theorem 3.6). Unlike the discrete case (Figure 2), ω(u) is now a smooth, non-increasing function rather than a step function. OT region (0, p): the instrument never pushes these high-propensity individuals out of treatment, so only the aggregate distribution µ1,p is identified; the tight bound requires countermonotone quantile coupling. LIV region [p, p]: the propensity score has full support on this interval, so the standard LIV derivative point-identifies E[Y (1) | U = u] for every u; the bound contribution is exact. Trivial bound (p, 1]: Y (1) is never observed; the lower bound assigns ymin where ω(u) ⩾ 0 and ymax where ω(u) < 0. The top panel shows the smooth ω(u); the bottom row gives the bound contribution per region.

Figure 4: IVOT versus IVMTE identified sets for the policy effect θα = E[Y qα − Y ] across policy shift α ∈ [−0.12, 0.12]. The solid line denotes the ground truth. Shaded ribbons show 95% confidence intervals: light orange for IVMTE and light blue for IVOT. IVOT bounds are uniformly tighter than IVMTE bounds in both the continuous (left) and discrete (right) instrument settings.
Table 5: Synthetic experiment (discrete instrument): IVOT vs. IVMTE bounds for θα = E[Y qα − Y ]. Coverage = 1 for all α.

Figure 2: Decomposition of the unit interval [0, 1] of the latent variable U for the sharp lower bound in Theorem 3.3 (K = 3 propensity levels). The key distinction is driven by where ω(u) drops. LIV regions (I0, I1): ω is constant on the entire interval because its step falls exactly at a propensity level pk; the integral therefore reduces to a directly identifiable conditional mean ωk Eµ1,k [Y ]. OT region (I2): ω has an interior step at q∗∈(p2, p3) (dotted guide), so the bound depends on how the mass of µ1,2 is distributed relative to q∗; the tight bound requires countermonotone quantile coupling. Trivial bound (I3): Y (1) is never observed; the lower bound assigns ymin where ω(u) ⩾ 0 and ymax where ω(u) < 0. The top panel shows the piecewise-constant ω(u); the bottom row gives the bound contribution per region.

Table 6: Bed net application: IVOT vs. IVMTE bounds for PRTEα = E[Y qα − Y ]/α at selected policy shifts α. The IVMTE point bounds reported in the table use degree-10 u-splines (degree-20 results are discussed in the main text and shown in Figure 5). The IVOT 95% CI is computed via the delta method (influence function); the IVMTE 95% CI is a backward confidence interval from the ivmte package based on the degree-20 specification.
